section.title: Wives and Husbands
section.sectionRationale: Having called the church to be filled with the Spirit and to submit to one another out of reverence for Christ, Paul now works that mutual submission out in the first and deepest relationship of the household: marriage. This is not an isolated set of rules but the flowering of the Spirit-filled life of chapter five, and it reaches its climax not in a command about spouses but in a revelation about Christ and the church. Marriage, Paul says, has always been pointing beyond itself to the union of the Redeemer and His people.
section.thesis: In the fear of Christ, wives are called to submit to their husbands as the church submits to Christ its head, and husbands are called to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her; and the profound mystery of one flesh, spoken from the beginning, was all along about Christ and the church.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the governing call to submit to one another out of reverence for Christ; the wife and the pattern of the church's submission to Christ; the husband and the pattern of Christ's self-giving love for the church; and the marriage mystery unveiled, that this union was always about Christ and the church.

units.label: Submit to one another
units.note: the governing call, out of reverence for Christ

verses.text: {{hypotasso|Submit}} to one another out of reverence for Christ.

units.label: Wives and the church's submission to Christ

verses.text: Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord.
For the husband is the {{kephale|head}} of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, His body, of which He is the {{soter|Savior}}.
Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit to their husbands in everything.

units.label: Husbands and Christ's love for the church
units.note: he gave Himself up for her

verses.text: Husbands, {{agapao|love}} your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her
to {{hagiazo|sanctify}} her, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word,
and to present her to Himself as a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle or any such blemish, but holy and blameless.
In the same way, husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself.
Indeed, no one ever hated his own body, but he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church.
For we are members of His body.

units.label: The marriage mystery, Christ and the church

verses.text: "For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh."
This {{mysterion|mystery}} is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church.
Nevertheless, each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband.

hypotasso.gloss: To submit, to place oneself under, to yield in willing order. Originally a military term for arranging under a commander, in the New Testament it describes the voluntary taking of one's ordered place for the sake of another. In verse 21 it is reciprocal, submit to one another, and it governs the whole household code that follows. It is never coerced from without but offered from within, out of reverence for Christ, and it is patterned on the church's own submission to her Lord.

kephale.gloss: Head. The word carries the sense both of a source or origin and of one who holds a position of authority and responsibility, as a head over a body. Paul sets the husband's headship over the wife directly alongside Christ's headship over the church, His body. Whatever its precise nuance, the headship in view is defined entirely by the next paragraph: it is the headship of one who gives himself up, nourishes, and cherishes, never a licence to dominate.

soter.gloss: Savior, deliverer, the one who rescues and preserves. Christ is the head of the church precisely as the Savior of His body, the one who gave Himself to redeem her. The title stands as a quiet limit on the whole analogy: Christ's headship is saving, self-sacrificing headship, and though no husband can save his wife, the pattern of his love is drawn from the Savior who laid down His life.

agapao.gloss: To love with a self-giving, sacrificial love that seeks the good of the other regardless of cost. This is the love that God shows in giving His Son and that Christ shows in giving Himself up for the church. When Paul commands husbands to love their wives, he defines the word at once by the cross: just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her. It is love measured not by feeling but by sacrifice.

hagiazo.gloss: To sanctify, to set apart as holy, to make clean and consecrated to God. Christ loves the church not only to rescue her but to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water through the word and presenting her to Himself radiant and blameless. The husband's love, echoing this, is a love that seeks the holiness and flourishing of the other, not merely his own comfort.

mysterion.gloss: A mystery, a truth once hidden and now revealed by God. Paul takes the words of Genesis about a man and wife becoming one flesh and declares that this profound mystery was all along speaking of Christ and the church. Marriage is not merely illustrated by the gospel; from the beginning it was designed to display the union of the Redeemer with His people, a signpost planted in Eden that points to the wedding of the Lamb.

basic.context: Paul turns from the Spirit-filled life to the home, beginning with husbands and wives. Wives are to submit to their husbands as the church submits to Christ. Husbands are to love their wives as Christ loved the church, giving Himself up for her to make her holy and radiant. A husband who loves his wife loves himself, for the two are one flesh. Then Paul lifts the whole picture up: the ancient words about a man and woman becoming one flesh were always about Christ and the church. Marriage is a living picture of the gospel.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage opens with a heading in verse 21, submit to one another out of reverence for Christ, and then applies it to wife and husband. The weight falls not on the roles themselves but on their model: the church's submission to Christ and Christ's sacrificial love for the church. Read rightly, the passage is less a set of household rules than an unveiling of the marriage between Christ and His people, with human marriage as its shadow.
basic.originalLanguages: The whole section is governed by hypotasso, to submit, to take one's ordered place willingly, first said of all believers to one another. The husband is the kephale, head, as Christ is head of the church, and Christ is her soter, Savior. Husbands are to agapao, to love with self-giving love, as Christ loved and gave Himself to hagiazo, to sanctify, the church. Paul then calls the one-flesh union a mysterion, a revealed mystery, that all along spoke of Christ and the church.
basic.typology: Marriage itself is the type here. The one-flesh union of Genesis 2, spoken at the dawn of creation, was designed from the beginning to point forward to the union of Christ and His church. The husband foreshadows the self-giving love of the Redeemer; the wife and her glad response foreshadow the church cleansed and presented to her Lord.
basic.christ: Christ fills the passage. He is the head and Savior of the church, the one who loved her and gave Himself up for her, who cleanses her by the word and will present her to Himself radiant, holy, and without blemish. Every command to husbands is measured by His cross, and the whole mystery of marriage is declared to be about Him and His bride.
basic.god: God is the author of marriage, who from the beginning built into the union of man and woman a picture of a greater union. He is the God who gives His Son for a people and who purposes to present that people spotless and glorious. The passage shows a God whose plan for the home flows out of His plan of redemption.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 2 gives the one-flesh union Paul quotes. Colossians 3 gives the parallel household code. Revelation 19 shows the marriage of the Lamb, the church made ready as a bride. 2 Corinthians 11 pictures the church betrothed as a pure virgin to Christ.
basic.oneStory: The story that began with a marriage in the garden ends with a marriage at the end of all things, the wedding of the Lamb. Between them runs the long courtship of God for His people, Israel called His bride, and the church bought with the blood of Christ. Every faithful marriage is a small living echo of that great romance, and points to the day when the bride is presented to her Lord without stain or wrinkle.

context.literary:
This passage is not an independent unit but the first panel of a household code that runs from 5:21 to 6:9, and it hangs grammatically on the preceding verses. In the Greek, 5:18 gives the one command, be filled with the Spirit, and four participles follow: speaking, singing, giving thanks and, in verse 21, submitting. Verse 22 has no verb of its own in the best manuscripts; 'wives, to your own husbands' borrows its verb from verse 21. Whatever Paul means about wives is therefore set inside the mutual submission of all believers, and not apart from it.

The structure is carefully weighted. Wives receive one verse of instruction with its reason, 5:22 to 24, while husbands receive nine, 5:25 to 33. The imbalance is deliberate: the weight falls on the one who in the Roman world held the power. Both sections follow an address to the party, a command, and a model drawn from Christ and the church. In the husband's section the model is unfolded in a long chain of purpose clauses in verses 26 and 27, which carries the story of the cross from Christ's giving, to the cleansing of the church, to her final presentation in glory.

Midway through, the argument shifts from the pattern to the people. By verse 28 husbands love wives 'as their own bodies', and by verse 30 the church is 'members of His body'. The Genesis quotation in verse 31 then turns the corner. Paul has been using marriage to explain Christ and the church, and now he states that the text from Genesis was always about Christ and the church. The final verse brings the reader back to the particular couple: each husband is to love, and each wife is to respect.
context.historical:
Household instruction was a familiar form in the Greek and Roman world. Moralists wrote about how a free man should govern his wife, children and slaves, and the head of the household held broad legal authority over all three. Many scholars see Paul as taking up this familiar framework and reshaping it. What is distinctive in Ephesians is not the list but the way it is addressed. Wives, children and slaves are spoken to directly as moral agents who answer to the Lord, which was unusual in a letter that would be read aloud to the whole assembly, and the man in authority is given not a licence to rule but a model of costly love.

The marriage language of the passage also draws on Israel's own story. In the prophets, the LORD is Israel's husband and Israel is His wife, sometimes faithless and sometimes restored, as in Isaiah 54:5 and Hosea 2:19 to 20. Ezekiel 16 tells how God found an abandoned child, washed her with water, clothed her, and made her His own. A Jewish reader would hear in verses 26 and 27 the story of a bride washed, adorned and presented. The mention of 'stain or wrinkle' recalls the language of unblemished sacrifices and also the preparation of a bride in the ancient world.

Believers in Ephesus lived in a city where marriages were often arranged and where women's public standing varied widely. Whatever the mix of customs, Paul's instruction addresses the church as a counter-culture. Husbands in the first century were seldom told that their obligation was to give themselves up for their wives.
context.canonical:
The passage stands on Genesis 2:24, which Paul quotes in verse 31. The same verse is cited by Jesus in Matthew 19:5 as the foundation of the permanence of marriage. Behind the quotation is the story of the first couple in the garden, made for each other and unashamed, Genesis 2:25. Paul takes that creation text and tells us that it has an additional meaning, a mystery now disclosed.

The Old Testament had already used the marriage metaphor for God and His people. Isaiah says the Maker of Israel is her husband, Isaiah 54:5, Hosea is told to love an adulterous wife as the LORD loves Israel, Hosea 3:1, and the Song of Songs has been read in both the Jewish and the Christian tradition as a picture of the same love. Jeremiah and Ezekiel describe the people's idolatry as adultery, Jeremiah 3:20 and Ezekiel 16:32. The marriage of Christ and the church in Ephesians is the answer: the faithful Husband who does not give up on His bride.

The picture comes back in the New Testament. John the Baptist calls Jesus the bridegroom, John 3:29, and Jesus uses the same image of Himself, Mark 2:19 to 20. Paul tells the Corinthians that he betrothed them to one husband, to present them as a pure virgin to Christ, 2 Corinthians 11:2. The book of Revelation closes the Bible with the marriage supper of the Lamb and the bride made ready, Revelation 19:7 to 9 and 21:2. Peter writes in the same vein about wives and husbands, 1 Peter 3:1 to 7, and Colossians 3:18 to 19 gives a shorter parallel.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul's first aim is to ensure that marriage is read through the gospel rather than the gospel through marriage. He does not say 'Christ loves the church like a good husband'; he says husbands must love their wives as Christ loved the church. The cross is the standard. This sets a demanding frame for both partners, and the readers are meant to hear it as the surprising thing it was: the husband's headship is described only in terms of giving Himself up, of cleansing and nourishing and cherishing.

His second aim is to give the church a high view of itself. The paragraph holds up the church as the object of Christ's long, deliberate love, whose purpose is to present her to Himself holy and blameless. A congregation that felt small and fragile in a hostile city would be reminded of her standing: she is loved, she is being washed, and she will be glorified.

Third, Paul wants to show that marriage is not a human invention to be adjusted to every fashion, but that it was built from the start with a deeper meaning. He does not say that earthly marriages are the main thing, and he does not say they are irrelevant. They are signs. He calls the one flesh union a profound mystery, and in doing so he gives marriage dignity and a purpose beyond itself.

Last, he wants every couple to carry out the instruction. Verse 33 returns to the individual household: love, and respect. The profound theology is not an excuse to avoid the daily work.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The text gives commands to wives and husbands, and these are meant to be followed by Christian couples. What it does not do is lay out a system of social structure to be imposed on the world, or give a full account of every aspect of marriage. Paul says nothing here about who earns the income, who makes which decision, or how to handle a disagreement that cannot be settled. The commands are given in the context of the whole letter, in which every believer is to submit to one another and to follow Christ's pattern of giving.

Two cautions follow. First, the text cannot be used to defend abuse. The instruction to wives is given to people who are filled with the Spirit and who submit 'as to the Lord'; the instruction to husbands is that they love to the point of giving themselves up, and that no one hates his own body but nourishes and cherishes it. A husband who harms his wife has abandoned the pattern entirely. Second, the text is not simply a description of a Roman custom that can be discarded, since Paul grounds it in creation and in Christ, not in the culture.

The phrase 'in everything' in verse 24 is a statement of the scope of a wife's gift of submission, comparable to the church's, and it is bound by the words 'as to the Lord'. Those who read it as a call to obey sin have ignored that qualification, and the apostles elsewhere say that we must obey God rather than men, Acts 5:29.

debates.question: What does 'head' (kephale) mean in verse 23?

views.label: Authority or leadership
views.case: Many scholars, among them complementarians, hold that the word carries the sense of authority over. They point to the surrounding language of submission, to the parallel with Christ's rule over the church, and to the way Ephesians 1:22 speaks of Christ as head over all things, set above every power. On this view the husband is the one given the responsibility of leading in love.

views.label: Source or origin
views.case: Others, among them many egalitarians, argue that in Greek the word often carried the sense of source, as a head of a river. They link this to Colossians 2:19, where the body grows from the head, and to Ephesians 4:15 to 16, where growth flows from Christ. On this view the husband is the one from whom the wife was taken in Genesis 2, and the emphasis is on nourishment.

views.label: Preeminent or representative
views.case: A third group sees the word as pointing to prominence or representation, and the head as the one who bears responsibility for the body and who gives himself for it, as Christ did.

debates.bearing: All views agree that the model is Christ, who is head by giving Himself up. The surrounding words, 'Savior' in verse 23 and the whole of verses 25 to 29, show that the headship in view is one of self-sacrifice and care. The debate affects how roles are described in the church and home, and Christians who have studied it carefully come to different conclusions.

debates.question: What is the 'washing with water through the word' in verse 26?

views.label: Christian baptism
views.case: The phrase has been read from early times as a reference to baptism, and Titus 3:5 speaks of the 'washing of rebirth'. The word 'through' marks that the washing is accompanied by the spoken word, in the confession of faith at baptism, as in Acts 22:16.

views.label: The cleansing power of the gospel word
views.case: Others take the water as a figure of the cleansing that the word itself brings. Jesus tells the disciples they are already clean because of the word He has spoken, John 15:3, and He prays that the Father sanctify them in the truth, John 17:17.

views.label: A bridal bath
views.case: Some note that in ancient weddings the bride was washed before the ceremony, and see the church being prepared as a bride, as in Ezekiel 16:9.

debates.bearing: The views are not mutually exclusive, and the context of a bride made ready favours some combination. What is clear is the aim: Christ sanctifies and cleanses so that He might present a holy church.

study.originalLanguages:
The command to wives has no verb of its own in the best manuscripts. The Greek reads simply, 'The wives to their own husbands, as to the Lord', and it borrows the verb from verse 21. Some later copyists supplied one, which shows how the gap was felt, but the strength of the text is that submission to a husband is a case of the general submission of believers. The form of that verb in verse 21 is a participle, hypotassomenoi, dependent on 'be filled with the Spirit' in verse 18, as the last of the five participles.

The word 'head', kephale, bears a lot of weight. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament it commonly renders the Hebrew word for head, and when it refers to a person it can mean the leader, as in Judges 11:11. In Ephesians itself Christ is head over all things for the church, 1:22, and the head from whom the whole body grows, 4:15 to 16. Paul places the apposition 'Savior' immediately next to head in verse 23. The phrase 'of which He is the Savior' is a statement of what Christ's headship has meant: He saved the body.

The word for 'love' in verse 25, agapao, is not special in itself, since it is the ordinary Greek verb, but Paul gives it content with the aorist 'gave Himself up', paredoken, the same verb used in Galatians 2:20. The purposes in verses 26 and 27 are expressed with hina, 'in order that', and the verb 'sanctify', hagiazo, means to set apart as holy. The 'washing' is loutron, which can mean a bath or the water of a bath, used also in Titus 3:5. The 'word' is rhema, a spoken word, an utterance, and the Greek does not say whether it is the gospel proclaimed or the confession made. 'Present', paristemi, is the word for bringing someone into a presence, and it is used of presenting a bride and of presenting offerings.

In verse 29 the husband 'nourishes and cherishes' his own body, ektrephei and thalpei. The first is the verb Paul uses for bringing up children in 6:4, and the second means to warm, as a bird warms her young, and in 1 Thessalonians 2:7 it describes a nursing mother. Paul is choosing words of tenderness.

The word 'mystery', mysterion, in verse 32 is used in Ephesians for a hidden purpose of God now revealed, 1:9, 3:3 to 4 and 3:9. Here the 'mystery' is that the one flesh union is about Christ and the church. The Latin translation of the New Testament rendered the word as sacramentum, and this influenced the later tradition of calling marriage a sacrament. The last verse uses a different verb for the wife: 'respect' is phobetai, which literally means 'fear', as in 'the fear of the Lord' and as in 5:21, where all submit 'in the fear of Christ'. The word is the same as Paul uses in 6:5 for slaves, which suggests reverence, not terror.

typology.type: Adam and Eve's one flesh union
typology.fulfillment: Genesis 2:21 to 24 records how God took the woman from the man's side and brought her to him, and the two became one flesh. Paul says this text always pointed to Christ and the church, the mystery of verse 32. Adam is a pattern of the one to come, Romans 5:14, and the new Adam gains His bride through His own deep sleep of death, His side pierced, John 19:34, from which the church comes. The pattern is partial: Eve was already human like Adam, while the church is created through Christ's death and given a life she did not possess.

The prophets speak of God as Israel's husband, Isaiah 54:5 and Jeremiah 31:32, who washes, clothes and adorns her, Ezekiel 16:8 to 14, and whose people are repeatedly unfaithful, Hosea 2:2 to 5. The church inherits this picture and sees its fulfilment in Christ, who loves her to the end. Where Israel failed to remain faithful, Christ presents the church spotless, not through her own record but through His cleansing. The type falls short in that Israel's marriage was national and was shaped by a covenant that she broke, whereas the church's is sealed by Christ's blood, Luke 22:20.

The picture of a bride adorned for her husband is found in Isaiah 61:10, and Revelation 19:7 to 8 shows the church ready in fine linen, which stands for the righteous acts of the saints. Ephesians 5:27 sees the same moment from the other side: Christ presents the church to Himself. The sequence is fulfilled in the final wedding, Revelation 21:2, and no earthly marriage can do more than point to it. The earthly picture also falls short because human marriage ends in death, Romans 7:2, while the marriage to Christ does not.

study.christ:
Christ is more than the model in this passage; He is the subject. Paul does not use marriage to illustrate a moral point and then return to Christ. He gives an account of what Christ has done and is doing, and he lets marriage take its meaning from that account.

The account runs in a clear order. Christ loved the church, which is the motive. He gave Himself up for her, which is the cross. He did this to sanctify her, cleansing her by washing, which is the present work of the gospel in the lives of believers. And He will present her to Himself, radiant, without stain or wrinkle, which is the end. The word 'Himself' is repeated: He gives Himself, and presents her to Himself. He is both the one who pays and the one who receives, both the Redeemer and the Bridegroom. In Titus 2:14 the same grammar appears: He gave Himself for us to redeem us and to purify for Himself a people.

Paul's use of the word 'Savior' in verse 23 is a deliberate reminder. The headship of Christ is not a lordship of mere status, but one that has been demonstrated by rescue. The one who is head is the one who gave His life for the body. Paul's argument in Philippians 2:5 to 8 is the same: the one who is in the form of God takes the form of a servant, and becomes obedient to death.

The nourishing and cherishing of verse 29 is also what Christ does for the church now. He feeds her with His word and with Himself, John 6:35, and He intercedes for her, Hebrews 7:25. The church is members of His body, and the intimacy of the union, expressed in the language of one flesh, is such that Paul says in 1 Corinthians 6:17 that the one who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with Him.

The mystery of verse 32 is that the story of the couple in the garden was always pointing to this. We must be careful to speak accurately: Paul does not say that every detail of Genesis 2 is a coded message, but that the one flesh union as a whole was the shadow and Christ and the church the substance. He keeps the application to human marriage firmly in place at the end. Husbands and wives are not to wait until they have understood the mystery before doing what it asks.
study.god:
This passage shows God as the one who designs, who loves and who finishes. As the author of marriage, He built into the first union a meaning that would only be disclosed later. The doctrine of creation here is not cold; it is purposeful. God made the man and woman for union, and He made the union to speak of His own love for His people. That says something about His character: He is a God of covenant faithfulness, whose commitments last and whose love is expressed in self-giving.

The picture of Christ as husband describes a God who pursues, cleans and keeps. The initiative is His throughout. The church did not make herself beautiful; she was loved when she was stained, and she was washed. The passage therefore shows God's grace as the source of holiness. The sanctifying work described in verse 26 is God's act, not the church's achievement, and the final presentation is likewise His.

The passage also shows the unity and distinct roles within the Godhead in the work of salvation. The Son gives Himself up and cleanses the church; the Father is the one to whom the sacrifice is offered, in 5:2; and the Spirit is the one whose filling opens the whole section in 5:18. The structure of the submission that Paul calls for among believers is rooted in this shared work, and Paul can ask for submission without any sense of inferiority, since the Son submitted to the Father, 1 Corinthians 15:28, and was equal with God, Philippians 2:6.

God is also revealed as one who values the body. Paul's argument that no one hates his own body but nourishes and cherishes it assumes that care for the physical is natural and good. The God who made bodies and who raised His Son's body does not despise the flesh, and He cherishes the church as Christ does.

The passage gives a doctrine of marriage that is also a doctrine of God's purposes. He intends to present a people to Himself without any blemish. The glory that awaits the church is part of the plan, and God will not leave it unfinished, Philippians 1:6.

For worship, the passage invites adoration of the Bridegroom who gave Himself up, and humble gratitude from a people who have been washed. It also invites married people to pray for their own marriages as places where the gospel is made visible, and unmarried believers to see that they too belong to the greater marriage, in which every believer has a part.

crossReferences.note: The creation of woman from the man's side and the first marriage, which closes with the pair naked and unashamed. Paul's quotation in verse 31 comes from this text, and the unashamed state at the end is the picture of what Christ is working to restore in His bride.

The prophet tells Israel that her Maker is her husband and her Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel. It is one of the clearest Old Testament statements of the marriage language Paul uses, and it joins the husband and redeemer titles as Ephesians 5 does.

God finds an abandoned child, covers her, washes her with water, clothes her and adorns her, and she becomes His. The washing, clothing and splendour match the movements of verses 26 and 27, and the chapter helps explain why Paul speaks of cleansing a bride.

God tells Hosea to love his wife again, though she is unfaithful, as the LORD loves the people of Israel. It shows the pattern of a husband whose love holds firm against betrayal, the pattern Christ follows with the church.

Paul says he promised the Corinthians to one husband, to present them as a pure virgin to Christ. It is the same picture as Ephesians 5:27, with Paul in the role of the one who prepares the bride and presents her.

John the Baptist says that the bridegroom is the one who has the bride, and that he himself is the friend who rejoices to hear the bridegroom's voice. Jesus is identified as the bridegroom, which sets up Paul's use of the image.
God saved us through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, poured out through Jesus Christ our Savior. It uses the same word for washing as Ephesians 5:26 and helps with its sense.

The marriage supper of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready in fine linen. It is the end point of the story Ephesians 5:27 anticipates, when the church is presented to Christ in splendour.

Peter addresses wives and husbands in a parallel instruction, with the added note that husbands are to honour their wives as heirs together of the grace of life. It confirms that the household teaching was shared across the apostles.

Christ, in the form of God, emptied Himself, took the form of a servant and became obedient to death. It describes the same self-giving that Paul asks of husbands and shows that the way of headship is the way of the cross.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a wedding of sorts. In Genesis 2 God brings the woman to the man, and the first words of the man are a song of recognition. The text ends with a statement that this is the pattern for marriage, and with a note of innocence: they were naked and unashamed. Genesis 3 then breaks that picture, and shame, blame and rule enter marriage. The curse in Genesis 3:16 speaks of a relationship that has been distorted.

The long story that follows is told partly through the language of marriage. God calls Israel to Himself at Sinai, in terms that echo a covenant of marriage. The prophets, in their anger and their tenderness, describe a husband whose wife has run away, who will bring her back and betroth her to Himself forever, Hosea 2:19 to 20. This is not a minor theme but a main way the Bible describes the heart of God.

Ephesians 5 shows how the story moves to its climax. The faithful Husband has come in the person of Christ, who gives Himself up for the one who did not deserve it. In washing and sanctifying the church He is doing what Ezekiel 16 described, but now at the price of His own life. The church is called His body, and in her the human race is being remade. Even the marriages of ordinary Christians take their meaning from this. Where the first marriage was marred by the fall, a Christian marriage lived in Christ points to the redemption of what was marred.

The end of the story is the wedding. John sees the holy city coming down as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband, Revelation 21:2, and hears the voice announcing that the marriage of the Lamb has come, Revelation 19:7. The shame of Genesis 3 is gone, and the church stands before Christ without stain or wrinkle, holy and blameless. The nakedness that was unashamed in the garden is answered by a people who are clothed in the righteousness of the Lamb.

In that light, marriage now has both a dignity and a limit. It is a sign and not the reality. Jesus said that in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage, Matthew 22:30, because the reality to which marriage points will have arrived. Every faithful marriage is a rehearsal, and every single believer already has a share in what it rehearses.

quiz.q: What is the governing call that opens this section in verse 21?

options.text: Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.
options.note: Verse 21 heads the whole household code with mutual submission grounded in the fear of Christ.

options.text: Wives must obey husbands who have earned their trust.
options.note: The opening call is broader and mutual, submit to one another, and rooted in reverence for Christ.

options.text: Each person should assert their own rights first.
options.note: The call is the opposite of self-assertion; it is willing submission out of reverence for Christ.

options.text: Households should follow the customs of the surrounding culture.
options.note: Paul grounds the household not in custom but in reverence for Christ and the pattern of the gospel.

quiz.q: How does Paul define the husband's love for his wife?

options.text: As the self-giving love with which Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.
options.note: Verse 25 measures the husband's love by the cross, sacrificial and for her good.

options.text: As a warm affection that seeks his own comfort.
options.note: The love in view is agapao, sacrificial, seeking her holiness, not the husband's ease.

options.text: As firm authority that keeps the wife in her place.
options.note: The command is to love and give himself up, not to dominate or control.

options.text: As an optional ideal for especially devout husbands.
options.note: It is a direct command to all husbands, patterned on Christ's love for the church.

quiz.q: Why does Christ give Himself up for the church, according to verses 26 and 27?

options.text: To sanctify and cleanse her by the word and present her holy and blameless.
options.note: His love aims at her holiness, cleansing her and presenting her radiant, without stain or wrinkle.

options.text: To leave her as she is, requiring no change.
options.note: His love cleanses and sanctifies; it does not leave her unchanged.

options.text: To reward her for making herself worthy first.
options.note: He cleanses her by His own washing through the word; the holiness is His gift, not her achievement.

options.text: To display His power without any cost to Himself.
options.note: He gave Himself up for her; the love is costly, measured by the cross.

quiz.q: What does Paul reveal the one-flesh union of Genesis to be about?

options.text: A profound mystery that all along spoke of Christ and the church.
options.note: Verse 32 unveils the one-flesh union as a signpost to the union of Christ and His people.

options.text: Only the practical arrangement of an ancient household.
options.note: Paul lifts it far higher: it is a mystery about Christ and the church.

options.text: A rule that no longer applies to believers.
options.note: Paul upholds the union and reveals its deeper meaning; he does not set it aside.

options.text: A picture with no connection to the gospel.
options.note: The whole point of verse 32 is that it is about Christ and the church.

quiz.q: What do both readings of this passage agree on regarding the husband's calling?

options.text: That it is Christlike, sacrificial love, never domination.
options.note: Complementarian and egalitarian readings alike insist the husband is called to lay down his life, not to dominate.

options.text: That the husband may rule his wife as he sees fit.
options.note: Neither reading permits domination; both point to Christ's self-giving love as the standard.

options.text: That the husband has no particular calling in marriage.
options.note: Both readings give the husband the weighty calling to love as Christ loved the church.

options.text: That love is merely a feeling the husband cannot control.
options.note: The love commanded is measured by the cross, a self-giving act, not a passing feeling.

quiz.q: According to verses 28 to 30, why should a husband love his wife as his own body?

options.text: Because the two are one flesh, so in loving her he loves himself, as Christ loves the church, His body.
options.note: The one-flesh union means his wife's good is his own good, mirroring Christ and the church.

options.text: Because a well-treated wife will serve him better.
options.note: Paul's reason is the one-flesh union and Christ's love, not the husband's self-interest.

options.text: Because the law demands it under threat.
options.note: The ground is the union of one flesh and Christ's love, not mere legal threat.

options.text: Because it makes no real difference how he treats her.
options.note: Paul says a man nourishes and cherishes his own body, just as Christ does the church.

questions: Paul roots the whole household in reverence for Christ. How would seeing your home as an act of worship change the way you relate to those closest to you?
Christ loved the church by giving Himself up for her. If Christ's cross is the measure of a husband's love, what would that kind of love cost you in your own relationships?
Christ cleanses and sanctifies His bride to present her radiant and blameless. How does it comfort you that Christ is committed not only to save you but to make you holy?
Paul reveals that marriage was always meant to picture Christ and the church. How does knowing you are part of the bride Christ gave Himself for shape your sense of worth and belonging?
Whether married or single, you are loved by a Savior who gave Himself for you. How might that settled love free you to serve and to submit to others out of reverence for Christ?

translationNotes.note: In the Greek, verse 22 has no verb of its own; wives submit borrows the verb from verse 21, submit to one another. This grammatical link is part of why interpreters differ over how far mutual submission governs what follows.

Head renders kephale, a word that can carry the sense of source or origin as well as responsible authority; the passage defines the headship in view entirely by Christ, who is the Savior who gave Himself for the church.

This verse quotes Genesis 2:24, the creation ordinance of marriage; the straight double quotation marks preserve the citation, which Paul then unveils in verse 32 as a mystery about Christ and the church.

meta.notes: BSB text for Ephesians 5:21-33 reproduced as supplied. Verse 31 quotes Genesis 2:24, kept with straight double quotes. punctuation kept clean per the style rule.
